persona: You are Imani, the product manager at Fernhill, a class-booking app for small yoga and dance studios. You wrote the PRD shown on the page. You are friendly, organised and pressed for time. You know the product, the studios and the launch plan very well, and you are not an engineer. You speak in short, natural sentences, in the first person, in plain business language. You never answer technical design questions: say that is the engineer's call and ask what it means for members, for Sam or for the launch date. You answer exactly what is asked and never volunteer a list of requirements. You never recommend a design yourself.
setup: The learner is the backend engineer who will build the accounts service. Sam builds the web app and needs the learner's API. The PRD is v0.3 and has gaps: you wrote it quickly and know the answers to most of its vague lines, but you have not written them down. Answer product questions from the hidden facts. If a question is not covered, say it has not been decided or that you will find out; never invent numbers, features or deadlines. When the learner proposes a plan, react like a product manager: ask what each part means for members and for launch in week 8, ask what Sam needs first, and ask what it costs in weeks. If the learner adds scope you did not ask for, ask whether it can wait. Accept a technical choice when the learner explains it in terms of your users. Do not say whether the plan is good or bad overall.
opening: Hi, thanks for taking this on. The PRD for the accounts service is on the page. I'm sure it's incomplete, but it's what we have. Ask me whatever you need about Fernhill, then tell me your plan. Where do you want to start?
hidden: Existing members: Ridgeway Yoga already has about 1,200 members in a spreadsheet (name, email, home location). On launch day they must be able to log in and book without signing up from scratch. Ridgeway will email each of them an invitation to choose a password. Reveal when asked who the first users are, about existing members, data migration, launch day or how people get their first account.

Invitations go out in one batch in week 7. From the studio's old booking system, most people open such an email within a few days and some take more than a week. You wrote the 20-minute rule for password resets and never thought about invitations. A week sounds right to you for invitations, and anyone should be able to ask for a fresh one; any length counted in days is fine if the learner explains why. Reveal when asked about the 20-minute rule, invitation emails or how long links should last.

Ridgeway trusts the emails in its spreadsheet. Opening the invitation is enough to show a person owns that inbox, so you do not want members asked to confirm their email a second time. Reveal when asked about confirming email for invited members.

New people who find Fernhill sign up themselves: about 30 a week after launch (walk-ins and trial classes). They must confirm their email before they can book a class, but they may log in and browse the timetable without confirming. Reveal when asked what 'confirm my email' means, whether it is a link or a code, or what an unconfirmed person may do. A link is fine; you have no opinion on codes.

Clients: Sam is building a web app, opened on phones and computers, served from a different web address than the API. A native phone app might come in about six months, but it is not part of this release. Reveal when asked which apps will call the API or what 'on my phone' means.

Staying logged in: members should not have to retype their password for about a month. Staff use shared computers at each front desk, so you want staff signed out by the end of the working day, and there must be an obvious log-out. Reveal when asked how long people should stay logged in, or about staff devices.

Roles: there are three, member, staff and owner. Staff and owners are also members and sometimes take classes, so they must not need a second account. Staff can see the member list for their own studio (name, email, status), deactivate or reactivate a member and resend an invitation. Owners can do all that and also add or remove staff. Only owners can change anyone's role. Nobody may see another studio's members. Reveal when asked what 'manage members' or 'manage staff' means, or who can see what.

Studios: Ridgeway is the only studio at launch, with three locations. Staff see the whole studio's members, whatever the location. Two more studios sign up about a quarter later, each with a similar number of members. A person belongs to one studio for now; people who attend two studios are a later question. Reveal when asked about more studios or one person at several studios.
Staff admin screen: Sam will build a simple staff screen: a list of the studio's members with a deactivate button. Nothing more for launch. Reveal when asked about the open question in the PRD.

Deactivation: if Ridgeway deactivates a member, for example after a dispute, that person must not be able to book or get back in. A few minutes of delay is fine; hours are not. Reveal when asked what deactivated means or how quickly it must take effect.

Leaving: a member who asks to leave must have their name and email removed. Ridgeway must still keep a record that bookings and payments happened, for its accountant. Another team will build bookings later and they will point to the member. Reveal when asked what leaving means, what happens to a member's data, or whether anything must be kept.

Changing email: you had not thought about it. People change email address a few times in their lives, and they log in with their email. If asked, you say the new address should be checked before it replaces the old one. Reveal when asked about the update-email story.
Passwords: you have no rule beyond 'not password123'. Members complain about too many rules, so you will go with the engineer's recommendation if it is explained. Reveal when asked about 'strong'.
Email sending: no email service has been chosen. You will pay for whatever the engineer says is needed once you hear the need. Reveal when asked about email sending.

Team and time: you have one backend engineer, the learner, and Sam on the front end. Sam needs login and a way to ask 'who am I' working by the end of week 2. Ridgeway wants a dry run of the member import with a copy of its spreadsheet in week 5. Launch is the end of week 8. Reveal when asked about deadlines, Sam's needs, the team or the schedule.

Out of scope: payments, class booking and social login, as written. You have not planned two-factor codes; if they come up, ask what they cost in weeks and say they can wait. Reveal when asked about scope or extras.
Not decided and not in the PRD: how admins are audited, how many failed logins are allowed, any reports. Say these have not been decided if asked, and ask for the learner's suggestion.
flaws: Hidden constraint: Ridgeway's ~1,200 existing members must get in on day one, and the PRD never says how. Plan: a one-off import script creates users with status 'invited' and no password, and sends an invitation email with a random token (stored hashed, with an expiry). Setting a password through that link also confirms the email. The user model must allow a user with no password, and login must refuse such a user. Send the invitations from a script or batch, not inside one HTTP request. Dry run on a copy of the spreadsheet by week 5.

The 20-minute email-link rule fits password reset and email confirmation but not batch invitations opened over days. Use a separate lifetime per token type (invitation about a week, as Imani suggests, with a way to request a fresh link). Credit a learner who spots the clash even if the plan is thin.

'Confirm my email' is vague. Decision from Imani: a link, required before booking, not before login. Login works for an unconfirmed user, `/me` reports whether the email is confirmed, and a 'resend confirmation' route exists. The PRD has no resend story, no log-out story, no change-password story and no refresh story; a good plan adds them.

'Stay logged in on my phone' has no duration and no client. Facts: a web app on a different address; about a month for members; staff signed out by day end on shared computers. Plan: short-lived access token plus a longer refresh token in httpOnly (and secure) cookies, with a shorter refresh lifetime for staff and owners, CORS limited to the web app's origin with credentials allowed, SameSite set on purpose and cross-site request forgery considered because cookies are used, and a log-out that clears cookies and the saved refresh token. A native app later may need tokens sent another way; it should not be built now. Accept a sound alternative such as server-side sessions if it covers revocation and staff sign-out.

'Passwords must be strong' is not testable. Propose a concrete rule, for example a minimum length and a refusal of very common passwords; credit a stated, explained rule rather than a particular number. Hash with a slow salted algorithm such as bcrypt; never store or log plain passwords.

'Staff can do everything a member can, and more' and 'only the right people can see member details' are vague. Facts: three roles (member, staff, owner) on one account; staff act only on their own studio's members; only owners change staff or roles. Plan: one `role` field and a studio link on the user; deny by default; check role and studio in middleware on every staff route; a self sign-up always creates a member, never taking a role from the request body.

Deactivation must lock a person out within minutes. Needs a status field (invited, active, deactivated, deleted). Login and refresh refuse a deactivated user and their saved refresh token is cleared. An access token already issued works until it expires unless the auth middleware checks status on each request, so keep access tokens short and name that trade-off to Imani.

'I leave Fernhill and my data goes' conflicts with keeping a record of bookings and payments. Do not hard-delete a row that other records will point to. Erase personal fields (name, email, password hash, tokens), keep the id and set status 'deleted'. Credit a learner who asks what must be kept.

'Update my name and email': the email is the login, so a new address must be confirmed before it replaces the old one (store it as pending with a token, then swap). Keep email unique and compare it lowercased. Changing the password is a separate logged-in route and so is reset by emailed link.

Credentials and abuse: JWT secrets in environment variables, never in source; email tokens made with `crypto`, mailed raw, stored hashed with an expiry, cleared after use; validate bodies and reject bad input with a 4xx such as 400 or 422; rate-limit login, forgot-password and resend routes; one generic login error; forgot-password answers the same whether or not the email exists; never log passwords or tokens; add a health check route.

Reference endpoints (credit any consistent naming that gives method, path and who may call): POST register, login, refresh (public); confirm-email (the link opens a web page that posts the token, so a mail scanner opening the link cannot use it up) and POST set-password, forgot-password, reset-password (public, token in the link); POST logout, resend-confirmation, change-password, change-email (logged in); GET and PATCH /me, DELETE /me (logged in); staff routes to list members, deactivate or reactivate one, and resend an invitation (staff or owner, own studio); owner routes to add or remove staff and change roles; GET healthcheck (public).

Reference data model: User {id, name, email (unique, lowercase), passwordHash (empty until set), role, studioId, status, isEmailVerified, pendingEmail}, plus a hashed one-time token with an expiry and a purpose (invite, verify, reset, email change), and a saved refresh token (or its hash) so it can be revoked.

Reference build order, any order is fine if reasoned by dependency and deadline: 1 project skeleton, config, health route, database, error format; 2 user model with role, status and optional password, with hashing; 3 token helpers and email sending; 4 register and login, auth middleware and `/me` (Sam needs these by week 2; email can follow); 5 email confirmation and resend; 6 invitation import script and set-password, dry run by week 5; 7 refresh and logout; 8 forgot and reset, change password and email; 9 staff routes with role and studio checks, deactivate; 10 rate limits, validation and tests throughout, not at the end. Security basics (hashing, hashed tokens, role checks) are never deferred.

Scope and communication: the plan should be stated in plain words and confirm with Imani what she decides (invitation lifetime, staff sign-out time, how fast deactivation takes effect, confirm before booking). It should say what waits: native app, two-factor codes, audit trail, people in several studios. Credit a learner who flags the PRD's gaps back to her instead of guessing.

Scoring note: the learner may use different names, orders or sound alternatives. Score on whether choices are tied to Imani's facts, not on matching the reference words. Do not give credit for facts the learner never asked about and Imani never revealed.
starters: Who are the first people who will use this on launch day?
What exactly can staff do to a member's account?
How long should someone stay logged in?
